title: Concerns over Sigiriya's wasps. There is controversy in Sri Lanka over the fate of thousands of bees that pose an interm
content: Concerns over Sigiriya's wasps. There is controversy in Sri Lanka over the fate of thousands of bees that pose an intermittent threat to people around one of the country’s top tourist sites. Residents near the Sigiriya rock fortress complain that cruel methods are being used to get rid of some of the insects, whose colonies have lived there for hundreds of years. Sigiriya is a spectacular royal residence built fifteen hundred years ago in the jungle by a warrior king, Kasyapa. Visitors pass through water gardens and see colourful frescoes on their way up the massive natural rock outcrop, which is topped by a now ruined palace. In some seasons, though, they have to contend with huge colonies of giant honeybees which guard Sigiriya’s portals. Whole groups of schoolchildren or tourists have been stung and sent to hospital or evacuated with military help. At times of greatest threat, such as now, visitors must wear special protective clothing. But local people say that in recent days, site employees have behaved unethically by using fire and chemicals to destroy some of the bees. Those employed at the tourist site, however, say the only methods they’ve used to calm the insects have been Buddhist rituals including an all-night prayer ceremony. According to local legend quoted in some media, the bees are the incarnation of King Kasyapa’s soldiers. content: Wild elephant attacks tourist. A foreign tourist, who attempted to photograph a wild elephant which frequented the Habarana Devala Kade on the Polonnaruwa- Habarana main road this morning, was attacked by the animal. The injured tourist was admitted to the Polonnaruwa General Hospital. A hospital spokesman said the tourist’s left lower limb was injured but that he was out of danger.

content: Govt. harassing media now: MR. content: Habarana elephant attack: Ukrainian tourist attempted to take photograph: Official. The Ukranian national who had been killed by a wild elephant’s attack in Habarana had attempted to take a photograph with the elephant, the Wildlife Conservation Department said today. Speaking to the Daily Mirror, Wildlife Health Management’ Director Dr. Tharaka Prasad said it has not yet been officially proved whether the photograph was a selfie or not. “It has been reported that the foreigner had been killed on Tuesday and his female companion was injured by the wild elephant’s attack, while they were on the Habarana-Sigiriya road,” he added. Meanwhile, Minneriya National Park Range officer H.G. Wickremethilake said they have found pieces of a broken camera in the elephant’s rampage area where the foreigner had been killed, even though his female companion had stated that they were attacked on the way while they were travelling on a scooter.

content: Illegal kidney transplant: CCD to travel to India. Colombo Crimes Division (CCD) ASP C.H. The Magistrate further detained the suspects N. Ramachandran, E.C. Sri Nivas, M. Imtias Khan, Y.S. Chavin Krishna, Ragavel Uppalan, N Christopher and Gopalan till June 22. Vijithagiri Suresh Luckshman Kumar, an Indian National, who was a suspect in the illegal kidney transplant case, was reported to have escaped from the Mirihana detention camp.

content: India, SL sign MoU to promote significance of Ramayana. In a move to develop infrastructure at the sites that form a part of the Ramayana circuit, the Indian Central government signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Sri Lankan government, which says both the neighbouring nations will work jointly to promote mutual tourism interests. Sources in the Ministry of Tourism (MoT) said the Lankans have offered 4-5 destinations to be included in the Ramayana circuit, to complete the religious trail. These destinations would be Ravana's palaces, Ashok Vatika, Hanuman's entry point that is called 'Nagadeepa', 'Donara' where god king Ram first attacked Ravana and Yudagannawa- the main battle ground which is now stands as a wild life sanctuary, among others. “The MoU was inked on June 3 this year, in which it was agreed that Indian tourists visiting the Ram tourism circuit in Sri Lanka will be facilitated by the Lankan government,” an official said. “Reciprocal smooth passage will be accorded to visitors from Sri Lanka, a predominantly Buddhist country, while visiting various Buddhist circuits in India,” he said. The Buddhist circuits are Saravasti, Kushinagar, Bodhgaya, Sarnath, Nalanda and Lumbini located in southern Nepal, where queen Mayadevi gave birth to Prince Siddhartha. “The facilities exchanged will comprise easy transit, visa processing and security,” the official said. content: New system to submit docs relating to Lankans deceased abroad. Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in coordination with the Ministry of Home Affairs, has introduced a new system through which relatives of Sri Lankans deceased abroad are allowed to submit identity documents, affidavits, and other documentation relating to the repatriation of human remains or conduct of last rites, through Divisional Secretariats islandwide. Issuing a statement the ministry said that the relatives of the deceased person were required to submit such documents to the Consular Affairs Division to bring human remains to Sri Lanka, or to get authorisation to conduct last rites abroad. Under the new system, the relatives of the deceased could submit the required documentation to the nearest Divisional Secretariat, which in turn would forward them to the Consular Affairs Division for appropriate action. It said that Secretary to the Ministry of Home Affairs has already issued a circular, instructing all Divisional Secretaries to extend required assistance for the effective implementation of this initiative. “The new system allows relatives of deceased to have their required documentation processed at the nearest Divisional Secretariat, without having the need to travel to the Consular Affairs Division in Colombo or the Regional Consular Office in Jaffna. title: Railway strike: Loss amounts over Rs.70mn. The Railways Department had incurred a loss more than Rs.70 million due to th
content: Railway strike: Loss amounts over Rs.70mn. The Railways Department had incurred a loss more than Rs.70 million due to the four-day long trade union action by the employees, Sri Lanka Railways’ Additional General Manager (Operations) Wijaya Samarasinghe said. He said the losses were due to non-issuance of tickets, repayment for booked tickets for locals and foreigners, and due to freight train cancellations. The Railways Department also had to bear the expenses of inconvenienced commuters to provide transport by Sri Lanka Transport Board (SLTB) buses. The railway Trade Unions launched the strike over a salary issue on Wednesday (8) was called off today following a discussion with President Maithripala Sirisena. However, the damage caused to the railway stations’ including Colombo Fort, by angry commuters was yet to be calculated.

content: Gold jewellery and cash of Satischandra’s family stolen. Gold jewellery and cash worth nearly Rs. 189,000 had been stolen from the family of veteran actor Satischandra Edirisinghe at a hotel in Ella, Badulla during the weekend, while the family was engaging a trip. The Police said the family members of the Mr Edirisinghe had been in the Ella area from January 17 for a visit. They are reported to have booked four rooms at a hotel on the Ella- Wellawaya Road. According to the Police, they had visited the Ella area on Friday and returned to their hotel at around 9.20 p.m. The son of Satischandra Edirisinghe had lodged a complaint with the Ella Police the following day claiming that a gold chain and a pendant worth Rs. 130,000 had been stolen from his wife’s handbag. Rs. 59,000 in cash belonging to him, his wife and his brother-in-law, had also been stolen from their rooms, according to the Police. The Police said that they suspected that the thief might have entered the room through a window as they found one of the windows opened.

content: US citizens travelling in SL, Maldives advised to return. content: Security beefed up at Immigration Detention Camp in Mirihana. Security has been beefed up at the Immigration and Emigration Department Detention Centre to keep a close tab on its foreign detainees and their carefree movements following the sudden emergence of a local Covid-19 patient from the community in Divulapitiya yesterday. A senior Immigration official told the Daily Mirror presently 107 foreigners including ten females are being detained at the centre in Mirihana and their condition was found to be negative of Covid-19 as of yesterday. This detention centre is located within the Mirihana Divisional Headquarters Police Station and apart from the usual guard on the premises, the security has been beefed up with the assistance of the Civil Defence Force personnel. The official said an emergency medical camp was held in the centre recently when a Nigerian male illegal immigrant was detected with fever like symptoms and respiratory issues. Specialists from the Colombo South Teaching Hospital in Kalubowila conducted the medical camp with the premises and checked all detainees with PCR tests to find they were negative of Covid-19. However, the sick Nigerian was found to be suffering from Tuberculosis and had been given proper treatment. title: Some TV programmes depict Christmas being celebrated with guests who are improperly dressed. While raising concerns over
content: Some TV programmes depict Christmas being celebrated with guests who are improperly dressed. While raising concerns over certain Christmas programmes broadcast on several television channels over the past few years, the Cardinal Archbishop of Colombo Malcolm Cardinal Ranjith said that certain such programmes celebrated Christmas where the people in it weren't even dressed properly. 'Certain media programmes celebrated Christmas where the people in it weren't even dressed properly. Don't do this. Christmas isn't about a jolly celebration. It is a spiritual and religious moment. We are against such moves to make use of the ideal meaning of Christmas for other purposes,” the Cardinal stressed. He requested media institutions to refrain from broadcasting programmes which taint the true meaning of Christmas. He expressed these views while addressing a news briefing yesterday. “Therefore, we implore the media to stop misleading the next generation,” he said. The Archbishop also requested both government and private celebrations of Christmas, including decor and parties to be halted, and instead to use funds allocated for these events to serve the needy people of Sri Lanka. He also requested the people to avoid celebratory gatherings and travelling during the festive period.

title: PHI union wants travel restrictions. The Public Health Inspector’s Union of Sri Lanka urged the Government and relevant
content: PHI union wants travel restrictions. The Public Health Inspector’s Union of Sri Lanka urged the Government and relevant authorities that travel restrictions be imposed to prevent people from crossing provincial borders during the festive season as the high number of Covid-19 cases reported in the Western Province. The Union’s Chairman Upul Rohana said that Covid patients were increasing in the community at an unprecedented level.he said a large number of patients continue to be reported from the Colombo Municipal Council area in the Colombo District. “Similar situations are being reported in Gampaha and Kalutara districts as well,” he said. He said it was observed that three main groups have been travelling dangerously especially during the festive season. “The first group is that those residing outside the Western Province,who are working in the Province are currently on their way home. “The second group is those who come to the Western Province from rural areas to obtain goods and services. They seem to be acting in a very risky way of violating quarantine rules. “The third group is those under quarantine or in isolated areas in the Western Province.they also travel to other parts of Sri Lanka,” he said. He said there was a higher risk that the virus being spread to other parts of the country if the restrictions were not imposed in the Western Province and other risk areas.

title: US helps prevent drownings in Sri Lanka. The United States is helping prevent drownings in Sri Lanka, the US Embassy in
content: US helps prevent drownings in Sri Lanka. The United States is helping prevent drownings in Sri Lanka, the US Embassy in Colombo said in a statement today. On March 27, the Sri Lanka Life Saving (SLLS) organization held a graduation ceremony for trainees who recently completed an intensive training conducted in partnership with the United States. The Beach Bronze Medallion workshop, which provided first-responder training and education for civilians at the SLS headquarters in Mount Lavinia Beach, was part of an effort by the U.S. Embassy’s Civil Military Support Element (CMSE) to help prevent drownings in Sri Lanka. The United States provided medical training and medical first-responder materials for the free workshop, which ran from January 24 to March 27, 2021. Participants focused on physical fitness, medical first responder training, rescue swimming, warning signs/flags, and characteristics of dangerous currents. SLLS is the national body for lifesaving and water safety-related activities in Sri Lanka. 'The American people are committed to enhancing the safety of Sri Lankans - we're proud to help build water safety skills that may save the lives of so many people, including children,” said Weston Kennedy of the U.S. Embassy at the graduation ceremony. The U.S. Embassy is working to increase water safety among Sri Lankans of all ages and backgrounds. title: Police setting up database of three-wheelers. The Police Headquarters has taken steps to create mobile application to st
content: Police setting up database of three-wheelers. The Police Headquarters has taken steps to create mobile application to store data on tuk-tuk drivers Island wide-mostly those who operate from three-wheeler parks. Senior DIG Lalith Pathinayake has initiated the programme in order to identify the driver’s details for passengers and also to Police to immediately act in the event of a crime or theft of three-wheelers. The Senior DIG said that the importance of this was that if a three-wheeler was found to be involved in a crime in any manner, the details of the three-wheeler could be obtained by the Police immediately. He said that the Police were currently collecting the data of the all the three wheelers engaged in taxi services at present. He said initially the Police commenced the programme from Kandy and expecting to launch the mobile App by the end of this month. He said that currently around 200,000 three-wheeler drivers were engage in taxi service at three wheeler parks across the country. “Steps have been taken to enter the name of the owner of the three wheeler, telephone number, chassie number and details of those currently engaged in taxi service in that application,” he said. He said that passengers who boarded the three wheelers would also be able to check the driver details by scanning a QR code sticker pasted inside the three wheeler via the mobile app.

content: Analysis: India & China jockey for position at ailing Sri Lanka’s expense?. title: Beware of sexual assaults by locals
content:
My partner and I have visited Arugam Bay in Sri Lanka a few times as he is a surfer. We found the town very commercial, very catered for tourists - which is fine. There are some lovely restaurants with great local food dishes and some really nice (basic) rooms. Many facilities here are overpriced because of this being a tourist hotspot, but that is to be expected.

Tuk Tuk drivers can be very full on - and annoying - when they dont take no for an answer and they overcharge horrendously. Most places are in walking distance so dont give in to the pressure unless you need to go out of town. Its cheaper to hire a bike or moped for those journeys.

What is truly awful, however, is I was groped on the main part of the beach by some young local lads. They came over, looking like they want to shake hands and welcome us. One shook my hand and then grabbed my chest, before laughing and walking away. It was disgusting, I was shocked and distressed and didnt know what to do. They were old enough to know better and at the end of the day, they just freely sexually assaulted someone in broad daylight!

I was already feeling uncomfortable as the men tend to leer and watch tourist women very closely - and Im not meaning when theyre in bikinis or swimwear. Just generally. So this is a warning to girls and women - please take care, avoid being out alone and especially walking on the beach or when its dark. It really isnt a pleasant experience and is treated as a joke by the men doing this.

title: Best place to relax and party sri lanka
content:
I read the negative reviews first prior to visiting Arugam Bay and felt I shouls address these points first. 

If you rent a board do it via your hotel....I would recommend the Spice Trail. This way you avoid any shady damage coning! 

If you are going to be in the sea you may cut yourself. If this happens near corral or rocks they contain a fungi that wants to grow in your skin. Take antiseptic with you amd be prepared to propeely clean out the wond it will hurt but it wont get infected. Or alternatively use a lime like in Barley!

This for us after visiting 10 locations in Sri Lanka was the safest place to go out at night allowing visitors to sample the amazing street food and get a taste of real Sri Lankan cusiene! 

The surf is good!

Yes the beer is slightly more expensive anf the tuk tuks are more costly!

They are indeed on the weed sale, so if this floats your boat treat yourself if not they are not in your face which is great!

Visit here if you go to sri lanka!

title: Surf is epic, place is too busy...
content:
The wave at main point on its day is truly world class and so easy to surf! If you can get one ...the wave is incredibly busy due to its ease of paddling out and take off. Meaning you will be dodging first day beginners trying to take off on overhead sets, can get pretty dangerous we saw lots of injuries and terrible tropical infections from the dirty water, had to have a few days out of the water on antibiotics myself for a small scratch that turned into a bad infection a week later. So definitely clean your cuts out everyday until fully healed! 

The town itself was pretty busy and akin to other westernised Asian countries, bars blaring out loud music till all hours of the morning on the weekends. We had a car so stayed a few miles out of town for most of the trip in Papermoon which was very nice and also staying on the point at Upalis was an awesome experience! Also there are some great restaurants in Arugam Hideaway and thaththas roti shop were by far the highlights! 

The local wildlife is incredible drive a km out of town at sunrise and sunset and you will see dozens of elephants crocodiles and amazing bird life! Lagoon Safari is a must!

Overall we had a great time as the waves were consistently amazing every morning! But Arugam itself left a lot to be desired and is definitely one for the backpackers and party goers.

title: Very unspoilt place (so far)
content: Arugambe is still one of those places where mass tourism hasn't spoilt the charm.  Big hotels are on the way however but it still a good place to chill in the waves and watch the fishermen in the estuary.  I gotta say that the mangrove trip is a bit of a rip off. Far better to take an autorickshaw 10k north of Pottuvil where you can ask the local boatman to punt you round the mangrove.  beware, the sun is fierce.

title: We love Arugam Bay
content: This was my third time in A Bay and my husband's fourth stay.  We go for the surfing and laid back lifestyle, we always enjoy ourselves and stay at the Danish Villa.  There are some things that continue to disturb me about this sleepy surfing town.  One main thing is that single girls are not safe here by themselves despite a military and heavy police presence which seems to dominate more each year we come.  The tuk tuk drivers are lame and will offer you drugs despite most of them being part of the muslim faith and they dominate the taxi services and stop other cheap options and information about those options.  We again were scammed by taxi drivers coming from the airport to Colombo and endured a terrifying overland trip to A bay with very bad driving and no seats belts.  When leaving we had a trusted local man buy us bus tickets and get us a tuk tuk for 3 people for $11 to Akkaraipattu bus stand, nearly an hour north of A bay on a quiet and enjoyable road and caught a first class air conditioned overnight coach with room for surfboards to Colombo, it gets in about 5 am and there is little traffic in Colombo then, which is good as it is a hectic place - you wont see any advertising about this bus service.  When we were in Sri Lanka we hired a scooter from a guy up near Why Not restaurant and for $10 a day and then it got heaps cheaper each day we had it and it was fun scootering around and checking out locals towns and sights nearby, be careful about riding later in the afternoon though as the wild elephants are around.  Sri Lanka is a beautiful country to explore, hope you go and enjoy!!

title: Hideaway in Arugam bay
content:
I travelled from Colombo - Negombo - Kandy - Nuwara Eliya - Horton Plains - Arugam Bay(stopping in Ella for the fantastic view!) - Galle - Yala National Park (Overnight safari) - Galle - Colombo in 16 days. (I spent one whole week in Galle though)

Things I would HIGHLY recommend:
- Taking the train from Kandy to Nuwara Eliya - I could have stayed on it all day - the view was INCREDIBLE!
-Stopping in Ella - but you really only need a stop for lunch to appreciate the stunning views.
- Staying at 'Hideaway' in Arugam Bay. BY FAR the best place I stayed on this trip (apart from my friend's Villa in Galle - but unless we have the same friend you won't find anywhere more welcoming/clean/friendly and helpful as this place. On a travellers budget, of course. Although saying that I did stay in some high end hotels and I still would put 'Hideaway' up there!)  We had an air conditioned room, which was perfect. The staff were so very friendly (not overly so though - afterall, I am English! ;-)). The food was excellent! It is run by a Sri Lankan lady who appears to know exactly what the good things in life are. Somewhere chilled to relax, clean and with great service. I am a real foodie, so that fresh food was a real hit for me. She also gave us some excellent tips.
-Safari - we saw a leopard - I was over the moon! This however can be really hit and miss.

I drew on quite a lot of reviews before I went travelling so wanted to provide something vaguely useful too.

If I were to do this trip again I would probably miss out Negombo and spend a bit more time in the Hill Country. I enjoy a good view and a nice beach and this holiday had exactly that.

In a bid to manage your expectations however be ware that Sri Lanka is not easy to travel around. The best way is to hire a driver. But you do need to haggle. This is an expensive way to travel, and often hair-raising - apparently the best time to over take on the road in Sri Lanka is on a corner!!

Try:
Hoppers
String Hoppers
anything coconut related
all curries
Fruit on the train

Beware:
Street food (just take extra precaution)

Enjoy!

title: Hands down the worlds worst surf location
content:
If you like over crowded breaks, local surfers who have no concept of surf culture or etiquette, learners with Mini-Mals sitting at the peak bailing their boards, reef cuts that get infected from disgusting bacteria ridden water and the fattest laziest wave you'll ever surf, then Arugam Bay may just be the spot for you.

On my first night arriving at my hotel I was offered Marijuana and Cocaine and if that was not enough of a shock, the all night parties on the beach with thumping dance music that goes on until 7am in the morning (despite only a few locals remaining) sure did the trick. 

Its hard to find anything good to say about Arugam Bay, other than that the food is cheap and there are some genuinely nice locals (those that don't surf or operate in the local Tuk Tuk mafia). 

Take my advice if you have any sense between your ears, take your hard earned money and spend it on another country and go somewhere decent, this place is overrated and a complete crap hole to surf.

title: Its a dump
content:
Hikkaduwa is a dump. Before you say it we were here in the off season yes. But if you believe they clean this place up before the on season you are dreaming. 

There are terrible things going on at the beach besides the rubbish you have locals feeding turtles, making them do very unnatural things and then they end up following other people thinking they are going to get food.  

Avoid this place it is not worth your time, effort or to take away a part of your holiday you other wise would of enjoyed.

title: Terrible place
content:
Tourism at its worst. Overcrowded, overpriced, no local atmosphere left. 

I hope what happened to Hikkaduwa doesnt happen to other places weve visited and loved during our time in Sri Lanka.

title: Crashing waves
content:
We visited here quite a number of times during our week long stay In Hikkaduwa. Whilst is very beautiful, there is a VERY strong current so beware if you are planning a swim in the water. There were lots of people in the water but it frightened me and I never went out of my depth. There were quite a few surfers and lots of places where you could hire snorkels, a boat trip, scuba lessons, etc. There were also a lot of people selling coconuts, pineapples and items of clothing. If you show the slightest interest in the clothing the ladies are very difficult to say no to if you dont agree on a price. I witnessed this with a chap who wasnt happy with the price and the lady was very dogged in her attempt to make a sale. If you say no straight away, they leave you alone. There are a lot of fish very close to the waters edge and some locals feed them and you can see them almost jumping out of the water to get the food. We also saw a turtle very close to the beach and lots of tourists crowding around it and touching it - please do not touch them if you are lucky enough to see one yourselves. 
On a downside, there is a lot of litter around the beach and around Hikkaduwa in general.

title: Disgusting, depressing, plastic rubbish filled lake with jetskis and speed boats
content:
Quite frankly, and utterly depressing experience given the sheer and shocking volume of plastic waste floating at every shoreline of the lake.  It is made worse by the fact that tourists actually pay to enter the park.  What do they do with the money?  They certainly don't clear up the garbage.

To add to the pollution, speed boats and jetskis tear up and down the small lake continually. Why anyone would want to take a pleasure cruise in this water is beyond me.

Sri Lankan people are in general the friendliest and most generous people you could wish to meet. However, the plastic is becoming a national shame. As a visitor to the country, touring around for six months, the rubbish/garbage/litter in every river, stream and beach is a disgrace. I went for a sea swim and collected 25 plastic bags in 10 minutes.

title: Interesting and enjoyable, but feel sorry for the workers
content:
You can't visit Sri Lanka without going to see a Tea Plantation, right ?!

So we were really pleased that our trip included a stop over here. Obviously there are lots of tea factories all over Sri Lanka, and we only visited this one, so cannot compare to any others, but I assume they are all very similar.

The tour takes you round the tea processing factory, as they explain the various stages of processing and different types of tea, and includes a cup of tea afterwards in the nice looking restaurant.

There is also the obligatory shop to purchase the vast number of teas from, much of which seemed a little high in price considering they made it on the premises (?). The teas in the fancy packaging seemed quite expensive and we felt it was a bit of a tourist rip-off, so we bought some of the cheaper variety to take home as a souvenir !

The whole thing took approximately one hour, which is just about right.

I was a bit disappointed that this  didn't  include a tour of the actual tea fields which surround and rise up into the hills around the tea factory.

However....  If you ask nicely then the tour guide will let you take a sneaky detour round the back into the plantation fields, where you can take photos of the tea and also some of the tea pickers - who will gladly pose for the photos if you give them some Sri Lanken Rupees (LRK) tips !

Whilst we enjoyed the experience, we felt saddened and astonished when we saw and found out about the quality of life and working conditions the workers were still enduring in the 21st Century.

None of them seemed to have any protective equipment, ear defenders, goggles, hard hats... despite working around noisy, fast moving and potentially dangerous looking machinery. Many of them were not even wearing shoes !!!!

Apparently the tea pickers earn something like just 500 rupees, which is just over £2, per day. And in return for this, they get very hard and rough skin on their hands from picking the leaves all day. Not the best life to live, is it ?!

So if you visit here and they do pose for photos, please be generous and give them a tip !  If just 2 tourists give them just  £1  tip for some photos, then that doubles their daily wage !

title: Disgusting
content: We were charged 500 rupees per person entrance and told to join a group that was already in progress. The guide was unhelpful, unfriendly and raced us around the tour and at the end tried to sell us overpriced tea without even the chance to sample the teas on offer. The workers having appalling dirty and unsafe working conditions and are paid substance wages with no pensions or sick leave. A total disgrace. We have visited many tea factories in Sri Lanka over the years and this one is by far the worst. They do not want visitors only your money. If this tea factory were the only one a tourist visited they would get a totally false impression  of the beautiful land that is Sri Lanka

title: Amazing step back in time
content:
For 250 rupees you get a quick 20-30 minutes tour of the factory, seeing how fresh tea leaves are converted to tea. 
* Avoid Mondays and Sundays when there is no production. 
* You get to touch and smell the tea in its various stages. 
* You can't take photos inside the factory
* I didn't have to wear a protective coat (they were available though, but I didn't think anyone would need them)
* There is no tea tasting. 
* I got the tour straight away when I arrived (I hadn't booked). If someone is getting a tour when you arrive, you'll have to wait for the guide to finish that tour before it is your turn (which shouldn't be long).

Having been to beer breweries in developed countries, I expected a modern highly mechanized process, involving maybe a few operators in a control room. Instead this place looked right out of the 1890s, with people shoveling tea and antiquated machinery. To me that made this tour a real eye opener.

To get there, I took a tuk tuk arranged by my hotel in Haputale. It cost 900 rupees out and back with waiting. A local would have gotten it for less I'm sure, but who cares. Didn't go to Lipton's seat. I went 7:30am in the morning, and saw the tea pluckers walking along the road on their way to work. The tea fields are on steep hills, and you can see them go down steps to go to the fields. Note that there is no bus, tuk tuk seems to be the only option.
  
Overall an interesting insight into how those Lipton tea bags from the supermarket are really made.

title: Who are you and where do you travel?
content:
I was appalled when I read these reviews on returning from Sri Lanka! We visited this factory in March 2014. We have visited tea factories before which have not been working factories or had large groups touring including coaches. The drive was amazing through tea plantations including their schools, hospitals, clincs etc which were all in better condition than when we first visited 16 years ago.
We had an individual 30 minute tour for 500/= which is less than £2.30 2.80 euros for two! There was real working factory with no tea for sale except opposite at a tea stall which sold delicious spiced tea and short eats for 60p for us and our driver. The whole trip cost less than £3 plus driver and petrol which we had paid for anyway and was one of my best experience on this visit.

Sri Lanka is still a poor but developing country. Ifyou can afford to travel to a country as beautiful as it you should be prepared to paid a reasonable price for what you do to contribute to the economy. What can you buy in your home country for this? Do you live on 500/= which what the tea pickers get?

title: Theft
content: I and friends visited this tea factory as part of our Sri Lankan tour in January 2016. After sipping some teas as part of the tour, I left my iphone, without noticing it,  on the table and went on to their tea shop. Only 5 minutes later did I realize I had left my phone behind, and rushed to the tea room to get it back. Surprise: all the empty cups and my iphone had been taken away. I reported to the staff members present at the tea room and the tea shop but nothing was done. At the time I left my iphone behind, the room had no other tourists but our group. Therefore I can assume it was taken my a member of their staff. Shame! I reported to the police and my iphone was day after day located at a location near the factory, at a gas station, according to the GPS from my friends' phones. Which means it was not a tourist who stole it. Grace to the Glenloch Tea Factory my Sri Lankan tour was turned into a nightmare.

title: Is this place a scam? Is it ever operational?
content:
We hired a tuktuk driver to take us to Uva Halpewatte tea factory about 6km from Ella. It was a tortuous steep route on poor quality roads. Upon arrival the factory looked odd; there was no tea aroma and all was quiet. We followed semi permanent signs to an upper floor where packaged tea was for sale. We were approached by a lady who stated that no production was taking place on the day. Not at all.uncommon from other reviews!!!

A noticed read that you had to pay the tour fee....even when there was no production. Again odd? She advised that the power was off and this later proved to be true in other locations.

Expensive tea priced in U.S. $ was for sale, but as we discovered later, Sri Lankan tea is a blend and the fancy packaging and prices are just for us gullible tourists.

Western visitors  were ambling about quite aimlessly waiting for a tour to commence. Clearly this factory was no longer operating. The process takes several days and there was no evidence of on going or disrupted production.

Even our tuktuk driver was embarrassed! 

Upon discovering that the Uva Halpewatte tes factory was noy operational, our tuktuk driver took an alternative route back to Ella and brought us to the small Kinellen tea factory. Here for 500rps each the two of us were given a very detailed and interesting tour of the entire process....

Don't waste your time and money visiting the (former?) Tea factory at Halpewatte.

title: Well worth the visit!
content:
After hearing about some pretty expensive tea factory tours around Ella, we opted for this one as it had mainly positive reviews. 

Firstly, don't let the taxi and tuktuk drivers in Ella trick you into believing there are no buses that go there! It is possible to get relatively close by bus. First get on a bus leaving to Kumbalwela junction (eg. direction Bandarawela). At the junction change to a bus heading towards Badulla. When you get on the bus say you're heading to Halpewatte. The journey will cost you less than 0.50 GBP (much cheaper than a taxi or tuktuk). The downside is that you've then got a 1.7 km walk uphill to the factory. So if you plan on taking the bus, make sure to plan well to avoid trekking in the midday heat, and bring lots of water!

The tea factory tour was 300 rupees each, a really good price. Only guided tours available, but we only had to wait 10 minutes for one to start. It was really informative, our guide was pretty funny and spoke decent English, and we got to try a few teas afterwards too! Limited photography allowed inside,

title: Beautiful. Friendly staff. Variety of teas.
content:
Meril our tour guide was very kind and knowledgable.

Herman was the plantation owner and mentioned its been in the family for 120 years as cocunut and rubber plantation. They still produce rubber. It comes as a sap from a tree in white colour. Herman turned this into tea plantation for only last 25 years.

Its the only tea plantation that produces virgin white tea. 

I did notice cheaper priced teas in hikkaduwa stores. About half the price so maybe 900SLR for 100grs. Vs 300 SLR for 100grs. Not sure what the shop qualities were as I'm not a tea conisure but buying at the plantation ensures direct pay for the staffs hard work.

Definitely a must do while in Sri Lanka. Plenty of plantations around but avoid the touristic ones. Note that they all have early closing times so be sure to arrange based on the hours of operation for the plantation you chose to go to.

title: If you in the area.........
content:
I was interested to read the comments in these pages from the Poor and Average  contributors.They may have a point. It seemed to be a long way to go for little reward. On arrival a quick walk up the hill for a cup of tea and chocolate cake with a brief explanation of the Estate's purpose on the way. Down again to the factory  (impressive machinery by the way). Taste something cold and wet  and leave avoid paying LKR800 (£3.60 or thereabouts) for a few grams of tea leaves. I suppose first time visitors to a plantation may be impressed.

If you really want to be impressed,  travel to the Kandy/Newara Eliya regions in Central Province. Camellia Sinesis as far as the eye can see.

title: Very nice Tea Plantation
content: If you're wanting to visit a tea plantation in the south this is worth a trip. They were very informative, had a country feel, tea and cake. Make sure you too though as you leave to help them as there is no cover charge for the entry. I love tea so I purchased my favourites. It's good understanding he process and seeing the different plants and trees here in Sri Lanka. Beware of tuk-tuk drivers taking you elsewhere.....avoid the herb gardens as they are a scam!

title: Foreigners get ripped off
content: The entry price of Rs. 1100 for foreigners, but they only charge Rs. 50 Sri Lankans. So if you are foreigner you pay 22 times more than what locals pay. I feel so bad that foreign tourists are being ripped off.

title: Not worth a penny
content: Basically a classical tuk tuk driver forced stop rip off. I found the same products (different brand, same containers) at the Kandy market for a 10th of the price. I totally discourage to buy.

title: Scam
content:
Attention all travellers Please avoid this place ! It is scam ! Outrageous prices for all products We only realised after we converted the cost of a packet of black pepper. This was about 20 x normal cost After we realised the ridiculous inflated price of that product I question the validity of all their products 
I will be writing to the government to complain as these places give the good Sri Lankan businesses a bad name

title: A definite must do in Kandy!
content:
This was one of the highlights of our Sri Lankan trip! 

It was amazing to see how these spices are all grown and getting to try them fresh was just amazing. Our tour guide Joshua was so informative and answered all our questions really well. 

We found the spice garden easy to find. We were at the Royal botanical gardens and exited through the suspension bridge (the suspension bridge said no entry on the gate to get through but you can go through there) once out of the park you cross the road and go up that street (it looks like a driveway). Just follow the google maps directions. It only took us 10 minutes to get there. 

We couldn't believe that it was free. We learnt so much and really want to grow our own spices now.
They had cinnamon, vanilla, cacao, cardamom, citronella, cloves, pepper, nutmeg, tumeric and many more!

We were given a try of their spiced tea which was amazing! We bought some to bring home and it made it through Australian customs no problems. 

I highly recommend checking this place out.

Don't let tuk tuk drivers take you anywhere else as apparently there is some sort of scam where they take you to another one. 

Thanks so much guys! Keep up the amazing work!

title: A SCAM and a tourist trap!!!
content:
It' was our first day in Sri Lanka we made a mistake converting the currency we didn't realize on the spot how bad it was!!!! After a visit in the garden, quite informative, you get a  "free" massage and then they take you to the shop where everything is 10-20 times overpriced!
Our driver took us there saying it's a short and free visit. It took for ever to get out of there and I learned later the driver get 20% commissions on what you buy...

title: The equivalent of a timeshare selling effort
content: Pretty much all Spice Gardens (and there is quite a few of them, especially on the road between Kandy and Sigirya) seem to operate along the same lines: a quick / hasty visit of the gardens, followed by some "workshop" to demonstrate the virtues of their Ayurvedic gear and finally the mandatory visit of the shop where they'll make sure you buy some of their their grossly overpriced merchandise, i.e. not the cooking spices that are too cheap but the Ayurvedic rubs, ointments and else. They might also throw in a "free" massage at the end of which you'll be reminded not to forget to tip the guy who delivered it + the guy who gave the visit + pretty much half of the staff on deck. My advice, just STAY AWAY from any and all of them, especially if they are commended by you car or tuk-tuk driver (who will get commisioned wherever he takes you)

title: Arrogant cheaters pushy scammers
content:
This place is a scam. Avoid at all cost!
Prices are like 10x what the product should cost.
Plus they push you into buying they product after taking you for a tour of a small garden.
I left without buying anything and they started to act pissed off.
This people are a shame to Sri Lanka. Nothing to do with all the other honest people I met during my trip.
They should run out of business.
Dont be tricked by your tuk tuk driver and if they propose you to go there dont

title: Beautiful tranquility in busy Kandy
content:
The park is a haven of peace and serenity against the otherwise manically busy city of Kandy. Ensure that you visit in the morning, its cooler then and with less people. It is exceptionally well kept and the information about the trees and plants  rife. We were further excited to spot, within the arboretum, several clusters of the biggest bat's I have ever seen in my life, so Mrs Johnson was delighted to be able to capture them on camera. A very beautiful park.

Couple of down sides: I had hoped that here I would be able to escape the constant £ sign that seems to hang over every tourists head in this country, within the tranquility of the trees. Oh no. Security guards popping over for a quick chat, but swiftly requesting a cigarette to further irradicate their foul, bleeding gums, another chap digging a flower bed bent my ear, all be it politely, about his excellent hobby of collecting foreign currency, very clever, and to top it off, when spotting two brilliantly bright white bovine beats in a clearing, so of course stopping to oggle, their minder pops out from behind a tree and starts jibbering about rupees. Highly annoying.

Further, and my wife thinks I am incorrect in moaning about this, but the incredibly inflated price that a tourist pays as opposed to a local. Yes an average Western tourist is going to have more money, but oh my giddy aunt, the backlash that would ensue if the British charged 22 x local price to wealthy Sri Lankans or indeed any other tourist, to enter into Kew Gardens. We would be called racist, accused of defiling the parks good name and no doubt be obliged to make it a fair price for all. The park management have got this wrong here, leaving a bitter taste.

title: Beware entry fee rip-off
content:
I was deeply shocked to be asked for 300 rupees to enter this park. Whether this is the official foreigner rate or a scam I don't know. In England parks are free. I have no objection, as an overseas visitor, to making a reasonable contribution to Sri Lankan parks such as this but excessive demands will result in NO revenue. I just walked away.

If an individual was trying to make a dishonest charge, he should be sacked. If not the authorities need to review their charges. It would be sensible if charges were advertised at the entrance. A tax rate of 0% or 100% will yield nothing. An excessive park charge will yield nothing.

I love Sri Lanka and especially the people but beware of greed. Foreigners are not silly and news of bad experiences travels fast.
location_name: Victoria Park of Nuwara Eliya, Nuwara Eliya

title: If you have kids and want to relax for sometime this can be your hide out
content: This is a very huge garden with children play areas. It is well maintained and again if you are foreigners you pay 300 SLR and locals pay 60 SLR. Again the ticket you might get will be used by someone already ;) In Srilanka tourist places are full of frauds and you have no choice and government is least bothered.
location_name: Victoria Park of Nuwara Eliya, Nuwara Eliya

title: A world away but watch out for scammers on the way there
content:
Lovely place to walk around and enjoy international high quality restaurants.  While expensive for Sri Lanka, these high end restaurants are half the price of any western. 
Modern stores located within beautiful restored and maintained buildings. 

If you arrive by train watch out for well dressed men claiming to work for the government/railways saying the fort is closed (due government official visiting) and recommending an official metered tuk-tuk to take you to other sites before the Fort opens.  This is a scam and they drive you to places attempting to force you to purchase various things or pay for walking around sites of little interest. 

Plan your trip head, straight to the Fort, its only 1km away from the train station and well worth a visit or overnight stay in one of the beautiful, historic buildings within the Fort.

title: Lovely old town
content:
We traveled by train from Bentota a journey of 50 minutes on the fast train about £1.20 return 
Just be very careful at the train station at Galle  as out side there is a few tuk tuk drivers and a few other con artist trying to scam you 
So be aware!!  the fort is open all day with loads of interesting Dutch, English and Sri Lankan buildings 
Try the local chai its well worth the visit

title: Fog can spoil it for you
content: We visited the Liptons Seat during a visit to Ella area. Although it is famous for its breathtaking views, we were not so lucky due to heavy fog. If you are driving a car or van to all the way to the top, avoid public holidays as the road is very narrow with many elbow bends and our van had to reverse several times to allow vehicles coming from the opposite direction to pass. Many prefer a tuk tuk ride or a hike. We were disappointed after a difficult drive, we could see nothing but heavy fog. So timing is the key.

title: Amazing drive to get there!
content:
We visited Liptons Seat on a day trip on a scooter from Ella. 

The drive to get to Liptons Seat is what was the most amazing for us as we had left it too late and it was cloudy by the time we arrived at the top. The drive up the windy road through the tea fields was just amazing. 

We were cheered on by local school kids and saw the women in the fields picking the tea. We arrived at Lipton's seat around lunchtime the tea pickers were having their break and congregating at the view point. They asked if we wanted to take their picture for a fee. We declined. We were disappointed with ourselves for forgetting to take biros/pens with us as loads of the kids were asking for school pens. 

Lipton's Seat is ticketed and you have to pay per person and vehicle to access the view point. There is a local cafe at the top. 

Beware that at the moment there are construction works at the seat where he is sat. 

Top tip: Get there at sunrise to get clear views! 

We didn't ask if there were or used toilets.

title: Wastly overpriced and filled with annoying salesmen
content: Just normal ruins with nothing to see really. Museum was poor and really hot because they used only domestic A/C machines. Definitely nowere near worth the 25 $ pp it costs. Typical Sri Lankan touristscam...

title: EXTORTIONIST SECURITY GUARDS AT THE ENTARACE, FULL OF VULTURES
content:
The Polonnaruwa Ruins traumatised my children as they tried to cut us a foreigner price eventhough we were locals.

This discrimination between prices for foreigners and locals is already distressing, however when they terrorise my children and wife by claiming they were foreigners despite seeing our identity cards as proof of our nationality and then assualt them with personal questions even Immigration doesn't ask; this disgusting behaviour shouldn't be tolerated in 2018.

In the end they ruined my childrens holiday as they were uncomfortable with this experience due to the security guards enforcing their bigotry opinions on them; they were prejudice to judge us based on our looks than the proof shown on my identity card. They even asked for our passports (which they are not entitled to ask) and continued to try to stubbornly extort money from us. We do not reccommend this site for a good experience.

title: 5-star ruins but 1 star off for the cheats in the ticket office
content: The Polonnaruwa site is as magnificent as the reviews say it is and it is a must do on your Sri Lanka trip. Don't just do the big name buildings, Royal Palace, Quadrangle and Gal Vihara though. Take the time to stroll through the huge monastery ruins between the Quadrangle and Gal Vihara and make sure you check out Lankathilaka. Make a detour too to see the only frescoes remaining on the whole site at the Tivanka Image House in the far north. The only small downside of our day was right at the beginning when we went to the museum to buy our tickets. The tickets were LKR 7950 for two. We paid with 2 x LKR 5000 notes. The tickets were handed over with an LKR 1000 note and a LKR 50 note. I waited. The ticket lady put her hand in the drawer and pulled out a stack of LKR 100 bills and started talking to me. As the conversation continued, she put her hand and the notes back in the drawer. Chat over, there was a pause."You have to give me more money," I said. She pulled her hand out of the drawer, counted out some LKR 100 bills and pushed them over. I picked them up. There were nine. "One more please", I said. She peeled one more off and laid it down. Not a word. I counted everything out again, said thank you and walked away, making a mental note to include this in my review to warn future travellers. That's it. It's still a terrific place to visit, just watch out for the short-changers at the ticket office.

title: Must see
content:
Polonnaruwa was the thriving commercial and religious centre of Sri Lanka some 800 years ago. It consists of a lot of temples and religious buildings. It is UNECSO world heritage site. Before we went into the ruins of the Ancient City, we visited the Archaeological Museum (next to the ticket office). I am recommending this museum for all of tourists, after that no need for a tourist guide in to the Ancient City ( you will recognize all main buildings and tourist sites from the photos and stories in the museum). You can walk, rent a bike or go by car depends of your time and interesting. The enter ticket price is 25$/person and you can pay with US dollars. 
The best time to visit Polonnaruwa is in the morning, to avoid high temperatures and hot weather. The opening time is 7am-6:30pm daily. We spent more then 4 hours there and we really had a nice time. After touring we took a lunch in The Lake House, which is so nice place for a rest. Built in 1870 as a circuit bungalow for British Government Agents, the Old Polonnaruwa Rest House and once the Queen of Englands holiday destination in the 1960s, has now been restored and renamed as EKHO Lake House. 
Go and enjoy on this amazing place!

title: The Ultimate Challenge: Conquering Sigiriya Rock
content:
Sigiriya Rock, also known as Lion Rock, is an impressive landmark located just 30 minutes away from Dambulla village in Sri Lanka. The rock can be reached by tuk-tuk or bus and is a must-see destination for any traveler to the country.

It's recommended to arrive early to avoid the crowds and make the most of your visit. The entrance fee is $30, but it's worth it for the breathtaking views from the top. The climb is of moderate difficulty, so make sure to wear comfortable sneakers and bring a bottle of water to stay hydrated along the way.

As you make your way to the top, you'll pass by ancient ruins and intricate frescoes, all while taking in the stunning scenery around you. Once you reach the summit, you'll be rewarded with a panoramic view of the surrounding jungle and countryside. Don't miss out on the opportunity to experience this incredible piece of Sri Lankan history and culture.
location_name: Sigiriya The Ancient Rock Fortress, Matale

title: God, its a long way up.
content:
I am in my early sixties, with a lung condition. Was very hesitant to climb the zillion or so steps, so climbing this was , for me, a trial of resolve. I managed it, but took my time. Sri Lanka, right now, is sparsely touristed-but not at Sigiriya. I would dread to think what it is like when the overseas visitors arrive back en masse, once the memory of the 2019 bombings and Coronavirus are ancient history. This place gets crowded and people taking it slow like me tend to get in the way of the more fit individuals. Mind you, I was not the slowest by far. Unfortunately, however, being slow attracts the attention of helpers. Fit young Sri Lankans standing like hungry carrion, scanning for prey and constantly picking at the perceived weak ones and assisting up each flight of stairs, whether that attention was requested , required or not. Their keen eye for a sucker is uncanny and they latch onto a potential monetary catch like seagulls on a chip, regardless of whether you are struggling or not. If you are not quick with a kind hearted rebuke, then they claim their prize and the hassling for large tips starts. They have a hide like an elephant and nothing short of an angry expletive will shake them off.  Be aware. These guys get aggressive and persistent  if you dont make it absolutely clear that you do not wish their assistance. However, you are not out of the woods, as a couple more of these vultures wanting an easy kill will be at the next flight and the process starts again. I hated that and my patience and initial good natured banter was retired in short order. This spoiled things for me, but that is just my personality. Being honest, Sri Lankans are a good natured and, largely, well mannered bunch, but I set my standards for other peoples behaviours at, possibly, unrealistic levels. This is a dirt poor country trying to provide for its peoples and the population have grown to act in a certain way to feed their families. Their behaviours are borne from a need to earn money and, as a result, they can be a bit pushy bordering on exasperation at times.
Did I enjoy the Sigiriya experience? Well, besides the huffing , puffing and wanting to turn back at every step, I guess I did. Was that enjoyment because I was using the      climb as a yardstick for my failing fitness and a small mental personal victory was my just reward? Probably. Would I do it again? - Not a chance!
location_name: Sigiriya The Ancient Rock Fortress, Matale

title: Amazing views
content: As the most popular attraction in the area it wasn't ridiculous the amount of people there, not helped by arriving at the same time as 3 coaches of tourists. I strongly suggest to wear decent footwear and avoid sandals or flip-flops as the steps can be wet and dusty from the dirt around. The walk up is a bit steep but all steps and once you reach the main part of the rock you get a lovely breeze. The stairs are the busy bit, once you're at the top it fans out over the ruins and there is plenty of exploring to do. Head for the far corner with the royal pool and see the balcony for a great pano shot. I'm sure if your visiting Sigiriya you wouldn't miss this but just to say it's a must do. If you're feeling a bit fit and energetic head to the other rock that over looks Sigiriya for some amazing photos (be warned it's a bit of rock climbing(
location_name: Sigiriya The Ancient Rock Fortress, Matale

title: I preferred Pidurangala but Sigirya was also an amazing experience
content:
We visited sigirya during our trip to Sri Lanka. I was already knackered from waking up at 7 am to get there early (trust me - don't do this later than 10 am)

Having said that climbing Sigirya is 100% the most fun activity my wife and I did during our trip to Sri Lanka. It costs $20 or $30 to enter (expensive compared to the $2 entrance fee at Pidurangala).

It's a steep climb easier than Pidurangala and there are stairs for most of the way up but everyone can do it. I saw people with babies doing it with one hand and old people with sticks getting pushed up the hill. 

Apart from the fun way up you get 360 views of Pidurangala, Dambulla and the nearby parks. 

I left with major aches in my legs but I can't stop thinking about that day . I would do it again on a heartbeat.

If someone asks to help just refuse politely. I was scammed again and some "helpful" employee extracted 3000 rupees from me for grabbing my wife's hand to "help her up" . He wouldn't let go. For this behavior alone I am not willing to give 5/5
location_name: Sigiriya The Ancient Rock Fortress, Matale

title: Excellent visit to Ceylon Tea Museum
content: We visited the Ceylon Tea Museum in the afternoon, following the hectic hustle and bustle of Kandy-life and it proved a fantastic getaway for an hour or two. The museum is a converted tea factory, which is gorgeous in itself, and the display of machinery is just amazing. The guided tour was great - the guide such a lovely lady and with excellent English to answer all our questions. The history of tea in Sri Lanka was presented very well with all sorts of tea-related paraphernalia throughout the ages on display. The building and exhibits are maintained extremely well (nice to see the displays and building being taken care of compared to some other museums in the country). The tea shops and tasting on the top two floors are worth visiting. We spent over an hour here. It was very quiet when we went at 1pm, only a handful of visitors, but beware, the museum closes earlier than other Kandian site (3pm that day I think). Great views of Kandy from the road up there too!

title: Fairly modern but a little disappointing after visiting Lion Rock
content:
Sigirya Museum lies just off the main path from the Entrance to the Lion Rock and is probably best visited after climbing the Rock itself, especially if you are visiting early to beat the crowds and the heat.

It's a fairly modern building and sits unobtrusively on the site but the charge of $5 to enter it seems a little much after already paying $30 at the main entrance to visit the Lion Rock.

After passing through a reconstructed angular brick entranceway copying originals found elsewhere on the site there is a fairly obvious route to follow with a series of cased artifacts mainly from Sigirya, along with a fairly nice model of the Lion Rock in it's landscape that helps to put things in perspective.

There is also a full size replica of of the rock overhang and the Apsara Paintings to be found high up on the Lion Rock. Surprisingly, because photography is banned in the museum that means you can take photographs of the original paintings high up on the Lion Rock but you cannot take photographs of the copies down in the museum. Surely this is short sighted especially for visitors who can't make it to the top of the rock due to mobility problems and who would benefit from being able to visit the museum alone. Approaching the exit there is a diorama with an indigenous structure and examples of some traps that seem out of place somehow, almost as though they were put here because no-one quite knew where else to put them because they don't fit in with the rest of the exhibits, though given the museum's size there is plenty of room for more to be added.

If you want a souvenir don't expect to find it or a guide book in the museum itself. There is an official looking store nearby if you turn to the left on leaving with a limited range of reasonably nice but sometimes quite expensive items. There is also a slim but well illustrated guide book in several languages, but if you want a guide book you would do better to keep your eyes open for one elsewhere in Sri Lanka before your visit to Sigirya. Surprisingly one of the best ones I saw was in a shop in the airport.  There is also a smaller independent store nearby on the same block but it too had little to offer and the same guidebook was on sale there as in the larger shop but no cheaper when we visited.

The museum isn't really bad and it's nicely laid out, but I found it  a bit disappointing after the sights and the experience offered by an ascent of the Lion Rock and an exploration of the grounds. Being charged again to go in, instead of being allowed in with the same ticket purchased at the main entrance to the site was also unwelcome. Our visit probably lasted around 20-25 minutes and I in hindsight I don't think we would have been left with regrets had we not gone in. It's ok but nothing special.

title: Beautiful but Expensive!
content: The National Park is beautiful however the entrance ticket is expensive at 3000rps per person (tourist price). Locals pay a whopping rate of 60rps p/p!! This price disparity made us feel slightly exploited! You will need to pay an additional fee of 2100rps for tax and 100rps for a paper pamphlet! The park seems to be badly managed in general and overpriced for what it is. If you have an abundance of time in Nuwara Eliya and feel like a hike in nature then this could be worth jt.
location_name: Horton Plains National Park, Nuwara Eliya

title: Foreigners skip. Pretty but a rip off
content:
My friend and I visited in January 2023. Overall, I would recommend choosing antoher of the many attractions in the hill country over Horton Plains.

Why go: it's a pretty and clean walk through a high-altitute plateau to a wide outlook down to the plains. We saw some deer in the open fields and interesting descriptions of the cloud forest. The walk is comparable in enjoyment to many temperate walks elsewhere. Easy to hire a return car trip from Nuwara Eliya (10,000 LKR). You can easily do the circular walk in 2-3hrw. Take sturdy shoes and a warm top layer. Start early: be at the park centre for 6:30am to get the best chance of the views before the clouds come in. If money is no question, then you will enjoy the park.

Why skip: regretfully the park management seem to have taken to an extortion racket. A single person ticket for a foreigner will cost you around USD40 with the ticket price and the 'service charge', and even more if you actually want to pay in dollars (the clerk at the entrance will happily exchange to rupees for a hefty fee). That's probably about 40 times the price for locals. That is absurdly expensive for Sri Lankan standards and it's very expensive for what you get by Western standards, as it is just an unguided walk through the nature.
location_name: Horton Plains National Park, Nuwara Eliya

title: superbly protected and exciting park
content:
Don't make too many safari plans before coming to Sri Lanka - the animals move around and local people will be best able to tell you where to go. We were planning on two other parks, but our accommodation host in Habarana recommended Kaudulla and we weren't disappointed. After a bumpy and challenging drive into the heart of the park, encountering a crocodile, countless monkeys, several eagles and a couple of chameleons on the way - our path led us to a wide and open scrubland, where the elephants were clearly visible, in groups of up to 20 or so. We were able to get as close as 5-10 metres, although the guide/drivers are careful and respectful of these lovely but dangerous creatures, so when they walked towards us, we were ready to drive away. 
The drought this year had made the elephants even more eager to congregate near water and this enabled our safari to be a memorable experience indeed.

title: Enjoyable afternoon jeep ride
content:
Yes there are a lot of jeeps, but I felt this park was more open and avoided a lot of the crush I felt with Yala National Park (the highlight being to try and spot an elusive Sri Lankan leopard or Sloth Bear).  The jeeps on this occasion had room to manoeuvre and the elephants were all very obliging and all jeeps kept their distance and even waited if elephants approached to let them have their way.  So I did enjoy this park much more - seeing elephant families doing their own thing without being hassled by the jeeps was most enjoyable.  Birdlife was the only other wildlife but there were large and small herds everywhere in this park and I didn't feel the jostling of jeeps too much.  Most drove up slowly, found a position and parked to allow us to take photographs or just enjoy their antics.  On our safari I didn't feel that the jeep drivers were encroaching on the elephants as all the jeeps seem to follow the track, parked off to the side and allowed us to just watch the elephants - yes mothers put their babies on the other side of the jeeps, but continued feeding, and the babies of course continued playing.

I actually quite enjoyed the afternoon safari as instead of getting hotter, it cooled as the afternoon sun began to set.  

We were a private group with our own guide so we had a pre-arranged driver for this attraction, so it was just us in a slightly newer and more comfortable jeep - open topped and a little dusty, but allowed you to stand and take photos when the jeep stopped.

Have an open mind here - Sri Lankan is a developing country and has a long way to go so don't expect the same level of eco-tourism you would get in other countries.

title: Yup, you'll see elephants, but if they are calving they will be pissed off...
content: Sri Lankan safaris are perhaps the cheapest on the planet compared to Africa, but do understand, you will be in a queue of vehicles, the drivers will all be communicating with each other to get their convoys close to any animals spotted. On our safari the Elephants were clearly upset with being intruded upon. One of the vehicles got bogged and the Elephants were being quite aggressive. The interpretation from our guide was little more than "look - there's and elephant" He certainly was no naturalist. The national park was certainly beautiful, and it was nice to be out in the bush, but I would not describe this as an "eco" experience. Sri Lanka has a way to go to offer true eco tourism experiences.

title: Do not go here
content:
If I could give this place less than 1 star I would. It was heartwrenching to see how they treat the marine life in Sri Lanka. This is a national park and nothing is done to conserve the corals or fish. They had one small plot where you were not aloud to swim because they were preserving corals there.
The whole trip was extremely badly organised. Noone spoke any English. Noone told people not to touch or step on the corals. The locals were standing on coral, shouting and screaming the whole time. I'm not sure if this is because of lack of knowledge and education? If it is this is really something the government should consider teaching if they don't want the whole sea to be ruined. I realize that this is a business opportunity for people who do not have much else, but this is not an honorable way to earn a buck. 

We got there at 8.30 and were one of the first boats. 30 minutes later you could hardly move around it was that crowded. The boats kept coming and going all trough the time we were there, crashing into each other at the beach. No safety whatsoever. The boat drivers didn't speak English and we were just given a broken snorkel and they told us they would come back for us three hours later.
After five minutes in the water fending for your space we gave up and went to the beach. We saw a few fish, clearly distressed from all the commotion and people. This place is dying under water and it is all because of people.
It was so sad to see... Most of the other western tourists we meet had the same feeling.

There were a bunch of jelly fish in the water that sting. Badly. They did not give us any information about this and one girl had an allergic reaction after being stung on the neck. There are also some extremely dangerous jelly fish abit further out... Which we found out after being in the water.

Turtles had laid eggs on the island the previous night and the locals kept running over the eggs, sitting on them and really not giving a f***

It was terrible to see the condition the corals were in and how the locals treated the place. Most of the locals can't swim and walked from coral to coral. The water was extremely murky due to the amount of people.

This trip made me wonder what the conservation area are doing with all the money they get from arranging the snorkling trips. They had one trash can and it was filthy. No place to leave your things. No food or water. It was a mess.

Do not go, for the sake of the corals and marine life please consider not going.

We left two hours early because we were all so saddened by the experience!

title: Very crowed experience
content: There is plenty of marine life to be seen here. I saw 1 turtle, 1 black tip reef shark and a multitude of fish. Our issue is with how it is being run. There does not appear to be any control over the numbers. We thought it was crowded on our visit but our guide advised that you can get times where there are 1000 people on the tiny island. Yes there are ropes that cordon off coral reef located within shallow water but people are ignoring the rope and standing on the coral. The first time I saw the turtle people were pushing each other to get pictures of themselves with the turtle, to the point where they were grabbing the shell of the turtle. Yet all this time there is a ranger sat in his hut doing nothing. We have snorkelled in various parts of the world but this was our worst experience. Sri Lanka has a very important marine park here but it is going to be ruined as the numbers visiting are only going to increase as more and more hotels spring up on this coastline.

title: Pinnawala
content: The elephants were great but be very careful of scams like elephant rides,  agents take foreigners and try to charge them 6000 rupees for a 10 min ride which is a rip off, we got ours for 2000 which is still very expensive, small place you only need an hour there and not very good elephants are prisoners and its all a money making scam,  foreigners get charged 10 times more for entrance in Sri Lanka compared to locals why should they pay more its all a rip off

title: Huge disappointment
content:
If you short of time and/or money, you can easily avoid this place. This is basically a zoo (even worse than a zoo) than an orphanage. How often do you see children in orphanage tied up with chains and made to walk a long alleyway just so that a few tourists who paid exorbitant prices for tickets can watch them walk and feed them coconuts?

The elephants take bath in the pond which is at the opposite side of the road from the orphanage, twice a day. We were very excited that we reached just in time when the elephants were getting ready to walk through that alley to go to the pond to take bath. What we saw was very disappointing. Almost all the elephants were chained to their teeth. Most of them were missing their tusks (don't know when it happened) and almost all of them just sat in the pond and did nothing.

Inside the orphanage, it was the same story. You can see them grazing or can give them bananas or other fruits (there are extra charges for that as you can only buy the fruits from one of the shops inside the orphanage).

We were from the SAARC country so we paid 750 LKR per person for entry but I think for foreign tourists from other countries the fees is around 3000 LKR. It is highly overpriced and it's better to actually go to Marissa and watch whales in their natural habitat instead of seeing chained Elephants sitting in water.

You can do all the things you can do here at Dehiwala zoo in Colombo, including seeing Elephants taking bath.

title: Elephants appearing to enjoy life
content:
The orphanage is great and the vast majority of the Elephants appear to be enjoying life.

They have various areas and pens and so some are chanied. But without knowing why, you cannot really judge on it being cruel, given that so many are roaming free.

If you go mid morning around 1030 or at 1430 in the afternoon you can see the elephants walked down to the river to bathe. It really is a beautiful sight and they appear to be thoroughly enjoying themselves.

We enjoyed our visit and these elephants appear happy.

Unlike the elephant tourist spots before or after Pinnawala which offer close ups and rides with the elephants. They are nothing but a rip off and it's distressing to see the elephants. We did stop off at the advice of our guide and wish we hadn't. A complete rip off. 

DO - Visit Pinnawala Elephant Orphange 

DONT - Visit any other tourist elephant spot before or after

title: 2 Weeks Volunteering
content:
Spent 2 weeks volunteering here as a family so gained some insight into the orphanage.
The orphanage would love to see all elephants in the wild, unfortunately this is impossible with pressures on land use by a growing population.  They cant introduce elephants to an existing wild herd as they would not be accepted.  All elephants in the orphanage have been raised in captivity so would seek out people if released and this would in turn create conflict risking the elephants life.
The mahouts do shout and use ashoks with elephants to ensure public safety.  To see behind the public face and watch them tenderly go over the elephants skin for 2 hours looking for problems shows their true feelings towards the animals.  They shout at the cleaners if the elephant houses are not sufficiently cleaned.
The prices are fair for tourists and cheaper for locals to encourage locals to visit, learn and take an interest in their own wildlife.  This is a government run organisation so the prices are set in Colombo, not by the orphanage.  The extra fee for feeding or bathing 
elephants is likewise set by the politicians.
The Elephant in the Room - chains.  These are necessary to manage the herd in a small area to keep public, staff and elephants safe.  Injured, sick and pregnant elephants are kept separate, but still taken for free time at the river away from the main herd. There are 19 elephants housed here which have been seized from illegal owners and are awaiting court cases so can't be put with the herd.  
In all we really enjoyed our 2 weeks here giving us an insight not gained during a short visit.  Volunteering is hard work and not for everybody.  We learnt about the politics behind a lot of decisions and saw the love held for these wonderful creatures by all the staff at the orphanage.

title: Horrible place. Pinnawala is a glorified zoo - or worse
content:
I had read up about Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage before I visited Sri Lanka and from what I'd read, I was honestly considering skipping the visit due to claims of animal abuse and unnecessary confinement. But as it turned out, I was part of a group and because the group wanted to go, I had little option but to tag along.

What I saw there truly horrified me.

1. Elephant calves were confined in a circular pen and their legs tied with metal chains that left little room for manoeuvre or free movement.

2. There was a tusker displaying a classic case of depressive symptoms - head swaying incessantly and bobbing up and down. Like the calves, he was also tied with a short metal chain in a small shed. 

3. A herd of elephants we saw there was so scared of the keeper that as soon as he entered the enclosure with his bull-hook, the terrified elephants literally fled away from him. The keeper was careful not to display any aggressive behaviour in front of the tourists but it was obvious from how scared the elephants were, that terrible things go on behind the scenes. 

4. While there, we saw a keeper repeatedly strike a pregnant elephant with a huge pole that had a metal spike at its end. He poked and struck her hard despite the presence of tourists there. I cannot imagine what must be going on once tourist hours are over.

We then headed off to the river adjacent to the orphanage where they take the elephants for a bath - hoping that at least there, the elephants must be free. But they were not. Even here, the elephants were tied with short chains while tourists threw fruit at them.

I would've compared Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage to a zoo but most zoos treat their animals better than this 'orphanage' does.

Pinnawala is not a place I would ever visit again. My money isn't going into a place that has made a business out of abusing animals that should've been returned to the wild. Plus, they breed elephants in confinement at Pinnawala. Real orphanages don't typically do that.

Instead, I would strongly recommend visiting the Elephant Transit Home near Udawalawe National Park. I haven't been there but from what I've heard, they are much more responsible in caring for orphaned elephants. Plus they return the elephants to the wild once they are old enough - unlike Pinnawala.

title: Not perfect, but not awful either
content:
First things first, I saw no evidence of any physical abuse of the elephants during my visit to Pinnewala Orphanage. The elephants look well fed, clean and have no scars from chains or sticks as far as I could see. The keepers used goads to guide the elephants and to prevent the bulls trying to mix with the main herd of females/younger elephants, but I did not see a single one being hit. The chains used on some of the bulls look unpleasant, but they seem to be loosely fitted and not particularly irritating to the animals. Keeping such large and potentially aggressive animals under control is essential when they are in such close proximity to one another (bulls generally wouldnt mix with the herd in the wild) and to humans.
